==English==

===Etymology===
{{etymon|en|:inh|enm:accepten}}
First attested about 1380. From {{inh|en|enm|accepten}}, borrowed from {{der|en|fro|accepter}}, or directly from {{der|en|la|accepto|acceptō, acceptāre|receive}}, [[frequentative]] of {{m|la|accipiō}}, formed from {{m|la|ad-}} + {{m|la|capiō||to take}}. Displaced native {{ncog|ang|onfōn}}.

===Verb===
{{wikidata lexeme|L5421}}
{{en-verb}}

# {{lb|en|transitive}} To [[receive]], especially with a [[consent]], with [[favour]], or with [[approval]].
#* {{RQ:King James Version|book=Psalms|chapter=20|verse=3|passage=Remember all thy offerings, and '''accept''' thy burnt sacrifice.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|author=w:Joseph Addison|date=1714-08-25|chapter=The Sequel of the Story of Shalum and Hilpa|title={{w|The Spectator (1711)|The Spectator}}|number=585|newversion=republished in|year2=1721|title2=The Works of the Right Honourable Joseph Addison, Esq|volume2=4|location2=London|publisher2=Jacob Tonson|pageurl2=https://books.google.com/books?id=119Q-N9gi6MC&pg=PA112|page2=112|passage=The Chinese say, that a little time afterwards she '''accepted''' of a treat in one of the neighbouring hills to which Shalum had invited her.}}
#* {{RQ:Bulwer-Lytton Zanoni|volume=I|chapter=III|page=151|passage=I bid thee banish from thy heart all thought of me, but as one whom the Future cries aloud to thee to avoid. Glyndon, if thou '''acceptest''' his homage, will love thee till the tomb closes upon both.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To [[take up]] something [[given]], or [[submit]] to something [[imposed]], either [[willingly]] or [[reluctantly]].
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To [[admit]] to a place or a group.
#: {{ux|en|The Boy Scouts were going to '''accept''' him as a member.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To regard as proper, usual, true, or to believe in.
#: {{ux|en|I '''accept''' the notion that Christ lived.}}
#: {{ux|en|I can't '''accept''' nothing being done about the problem and your standing idly by.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To receive as adequate or satisfactory.
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To receive or [[admit]] to; to [[agree]] to; to [[assent]] to; to [[submit]] to.
#: {{ux|en|I '''accept''' your proposal, amendment, or excuse.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To [[endure]] patiently.
#: {{ux|en|I '''accept''' my punishment.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To acknowledge patiently without [[opposition]] or [[resistance]].
#: {{ux|en|We need to '''accept''' the fact that restaurants are closed due to COVID-19 and that no amount of wishing or screaming will make them reopen any sooner.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive|legal|business}} To agree to pay.
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To receive [[officially]].
#: {{co|en|to '''accept''' the report of a committee}}
# {{lb|en|intransitive}} To receive something willingly.
# {{lb|en|Philippines}} To do a service done by an establishment.
#: {{ux|en|We '''accept''' repairs.}}
#: {{ux|en|We '''accept''' bookbinding.}}

That's backed up by a 2011 report on Aboriginal homelands by Amnesty International that found that living on homelands was connected to better health outcomes and drug rehabilitation.}} # {{senseid|en|country music, elliptically}} {{ellipsis of|en|country music}}. {{defdate|from 20th c.}} #: {{ux|en|a '''country''' song}} #: {{ux|en|a '''country''' singer}} #: {{ux|en|a '''country''' festival}} # {{senseid|en|spirit of country folkways}} {{lb|en|informal}} The [[spirit#Noun|spirit]] of the [[#English:_the country, rural area, as opposed to the town or city|country]] (rural places): the spirit of country [[folkway]]s; those folkways. #: {{collocation|en|You can take the boy out of the country, but you can't take the '''country''' out of the boy.}} # {{senseid|en|rock through which a vein of ore or coal runs}} {{lb|en|mining}} The [[rock]] through which a [[vein]] of [[ore]] or [[coal]] runs. #: {{cot|en|gangue#Noun|overburden#Noun}} ====Usage notes==== The geographical sense of "country" usually refers to a [[sovereign state]], that is, a nation with no administrative dependence on another one, which is the definition adopted in most world maps. =====Usage notes=====
* This is a [[catenative verb]] that takes the ''gerund [[-ing]]'' to indicate the ending action (''stop thinking''), or the ''to'' infinitive to indicate the purpose of the interruption (''stop to think''). See [[Appendix:English_catenative_verbs#Difference_in_meaning|Appendix:English catenative verbs]] for more information.
* When used causatively, the verb can either be followed directly by its dependent clause (for example, ''to stop them exploding'') or take a helper word, usually ''[[from]]'', before the clause (''to stop them from exploding'').  The former usage is more common in Britain, and the latter usage  more common in America.
